Nice. Thank you for providing the link of the original source. I recommend that you use JDownloader if you need to rip anything off of the internet. JDownloader is an open-source tool that allows you to download files of interest directly from any of thousands of sites. You should really check it out.

Also, Handbrake is great but you should also consider using FFmpeg if you want more control over your video encoding/decoding. I've been using FFmpeg for a few years now and at one point I actually got interested in downsizing videos to extremely small file sizes so that I could try fitting entire cartoon episodes (about 25 min long) into a 16 MB file. This was because 16 MB was the file limit on 8kun (what was previously known as 8chan) and I wanted to contribute episodes for TV show threads.

I'm sure you probably already know that different types of video will have a different experience being compressed. A real life film with music won't compress as nicely as a PowerPoint presentation of static slides with only human voices. Thankfully, this video was mostly a PowerPoint presentation meaning it can turn out nicely.

As for how one should encode the video, you have two choices: use x264 and maintain compatibility across all systems, or go for the same quality at half the file size by using either x265 or VP9. I chose x264 because this video has enough of a max file size to be a decent enough video. As for the audio, we only want mono (why should we double the amount of data needed otherwise) and a codec that is best for voice (not music). A good codec to use that I chose is HE-AAC where HE just means this is a High Efficiency version of AAC (this is the best version of AAC to use for one channel). Next, you want to encode this video using two-passes as this will maximize the quality you get out of the video if you know it's going to have a fixed file size. Since you know the max file size you need to calculate the average bitrate this video will be encoded at. You can do this on Wolfram Alpha by just dividing the file size with the time. For 200 MB divided by 1h10m18s the resulting bit rate is 380 kbps. You need to remember that this bitrate is for both the audio and video. You wanna minimize the amount of bitrate that goes to audio and put all the rest to video. For audio of just people talking (1 person at a time) 10 kbps HE-AAC mono is plenty. You'd think that you could put the rest of the 370 kbps all towards video but unfortunately when you're targeting for small file sizes FFmpeg actually creates files that are slightly larger than what should be expected. That's why for this encode I targeted 340 kbps (I gave myself some decent amount of space under 200 MB so I wouldn't have to re-encode another time if FFmpeg still overshot).

The result is here: https://files.catbox.moe/971wh2.mp4

Just as an FYI your 57 min video had audio encoded at 128 kbps. The audio alone takes up 55 MB of the 200 MB limit. If you managed to grab the whole video you would've had the audio take up almost 70 MB of the 200 MB if you left it at that bit rate.
